transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. Um... I hope I'm explaining this okay, but I guess I'm here because I've been having a bit of a hard time lately. I mean, it's probably nothing major, but I just can't seem to shake this feeling that work isn't really safe anymore? 

And, um... I feel a little embarrassed even saying this out loud, but I just feel kind of... damaged now. Like, I recently got promoted, which is great, but it feels like that competent person who actually earned it just isn't really there anymore. Does that make sense? I'm sorry, I hope I'm not wasting your time with all this.
Can you tell me more about why you feel like work isn't safe anymore? Are there specific thoughts or fears that keep coming to mind about it?

Um, well... I know it probably sounds silly, because my office is actually very secure. I mean, they have good protocols and everything. But, um... it's just little things that happen there now. 

Like, if I hear the badge scanner beep at the main door, or... or if there are just heavy footsteps in the hallway outside my cubicle. Even if I get a late-night deployment alert on my phone, which is totally normal for my job. It's just... I don't know, it's like my body overreacts? My chest gets really tight, and I just suddenly see... um... I see the security guard on the floor again. It just kind of cuts through whatever I'm working on, and I feel like I'm right back in that moment. 

I'm really trying to just push through it and do my job, I promise. I know it's not rational to be scared of a badge scanner. Is that... is it normal to overreact to things like that? I hope I'm not making too big a deal out of it.
Can you tell me more about seeing the security guard again in your mind—when that happens, does it feel like you’re actually back in that moment, or can you tell it’s just a memory?

Um... well... I guess I know it's a memory, logically. Like, I know I'm sitting at my desk and I'm safe. But... um... for a second, it really does feel like I'm right back there. 

Like, my heart starts pounding and my hands get sweaty, and I just... I feel the same panic I felt that day. But I usually snap out of it pretty quick! I mean, I really try to just take a breath and remind myself where I am. It's not like I'm completely losing touch with reality or anything crazy like that. I hope that makes sense? I just... I know I shouldn't let it get to me so much.

Can you describe what happens when you see the security guard in your mind? Are these memories something that come up even when you’re not reminded of the event, or do they only happen when something triggers them?

Um... well, it's mostly when something sets it off, I think. Like I was saying before, it's usually those little things at work. The badge scanner beeping, or... or if I hear those heavy footsteps in the hallway. Even the deployment alerts on my phone. 

When those happen, it's just... it's like my chest gets really tight, and suddenly I just see the guard on the floor again. It just kind of cuts through whatever I'm doing, and for a second, I feel like I'm right back in that office. 

But, um... I don't think it happens completely out of nowhere very often? I mean, I really try to keep my mind busy so I don't dwell on it. I hope that's the right way to handle it? I just... I don't want to make it sound worse than it is, because I know I'm safe now. Does that answer your question okay?
Since that day, have you noticed that you often feel negative emotions like fear, anger, or guilt, especially when you're reminded of the event?

Um... I don't think so? I mean, I wouldn't say I feel angry or guilty or anything like that. I really try to just stay positive and focus on my work. 

I guess I do get a little scared sometimes, like I mentioned with the badge scanner and the footsteps... but it's not like I'm walking around terrified all day! I really do try to just push those feelings aside and keep going. I hope I'm doing the right thing by trying to stay upbeat about it? I just don't want to be one of those people who complains all the time, you know? I really am doing okay most of the time.
Since that day, have you found yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities because they remind you of what happened?

Um... well, maybe just a little bit? I mean, I still get all my work done, I promise! I really try not to let it affect my team or be an inconvenience to anyone. 

But... I guess I have started, um, trading some of my shifts lately. And I've been trying to push back on our late-night release windows when I can. It's just... walking through that main lobby after dark, it honestly makes me feel like I’m going to come apart. So I usually just take the side entrance now, or I'll work from home if my manager says it's an option. 

I figure as long as my productivity is still good and I'm doing my job, it's okay to make those little adjustments, right? I hope that doesn't sound like I'm just running away from things... I just thought it was the most professional way to handle it without making a fuss. Is that an okay way to deal with it?
Since that day, have you noticed that you’ve been more down, hopeless, or unable to enjoy the things you used to, even outside of work?

Um... no, not really. I mean, I try to keep my spirits up! I know it's important to stay positive, so I really make an effort not to let myself get down about things. 

I still do all my normal stuff on the weekends, like seeing my friends and keeping up with my hobbies. I wouldn't want to be a downer for anyone else, so I just try to appreciate the good things in my life. I mean, I have a great job and everything, so I really have no reason to feel hopeless, right? I think I'm doing pretty well with keeping a good attitude about it all. Does that sound like a healthy way to look at it?
